'Loud noises' and possibly 'happy families' can occur idiosyncratically, but a medical examination trigger is clinically disconnected from stalking unless there is additional trauma content not represented elsewhere. This makes the trigger set less coherent with the trauma type and formulation.

vignette:
Nina, a 38-year-old stockbroker of South Eastern Asian descent, had always dedicated herself to her career with a fervor unmatched by her peers. Her office was a whirlwind of numbers and fast-paced decisions, yet behind the professional façade, a darker reality gnawed at her. It had been nearly a year since she had experienced the trauma that shattered her sense of safety. She had been stalked by an ex-boyfriend, a situation that escalated from unwanted text messages to terrifying encounters. One evening, he had shown up uninvited at her favorite bar, his presence commanding and unsettling. She remembered feeling a wave of icy dread wash over her; it was as if time had stopped. The intense fear that enveloped her that night now felt unreal, a story so extreme that she often questioned whether it had truly happened to her.

Since that incident, Nina’s life had changed dramatically. The once vibrant woman who thrived in a high-pressure environment now found herself retreating from social gatherings and avoiding places that reminded her of that dreadful evening. Loud noises became a particular trigger for her, as they would often jolt her back to the moment when she felt the world closing in around her. It was an involuntary reaction; a sudden crash of dishes in the office cafeteria could send her heart racing, reminding her of the chaos of that night. The menacing reality of her ex-boyfriend’s stalking felt as if it was happening all over again. The sensation of terror would rise within her, leaving her breathless and anxious.

In the months following the trauma, her memories began to haunt her in ways she hadn’t anticipated. Each time a memory surfaced, it felt like a fresh wound, and she found that the vividness of these recollections heightened her sensitivity to triggers around her, leading her to perceive threats even in mundane situations. Because the memory came back so vividly, even the most ordinary things—like the sound of a door slamming—felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore. The intrusive images left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off. Even when she tried to push them away, they would resurface involuntarily, as vivid as the night they occurred. These memories would seep into her daily life, transforming ordinary moments into sources of panic, as she became increasingly attuned to anything that could remind her of that night. These memories would often flood her mind unexpectedly, and with each recollection, ordinary sounds or situations transformed into reminders of her past trauma, amplifying her sense of danger. When recalling her encounters with him, particularly the last time he had confronted her, she would often feel as if she was right back in that moment, paralyzed by fear. This intense reliving of the past left her hyper-aware of her surroundings, so that even the sound of laughter from a nearby group would evoke feelings of anxiety, as if those joyous moments were reminders of her own vulnerability. The memories would trigger a cascade of anxiety, causing her to perceive the laughter not as innocent joy but as a threat, reinforcing her belief that danger lurked around every corner. After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore. The intensity of these memories heightened her perception of triggers, making even the faintest noise feel charged with the threat of her past experiences. As a result, each time she encountered a sound that echoed her trauma — like laughter or a door slamming — it ignited a visceral fear, as if the memories were dictating her sense of safety. It was this reliving of the event that kept her on high alert, constantly scanning her surroundings for any sign of threat. The sensation of fear was so profound that it would feel like a suffocating weight on her chest. Each recollection brought back the same terror she had felt at the time, and she would often find herself tearing up in the middle of meetings, struggling to maintain her composure. After the memory had surfaced, the mere sight of a group of friends laughing together would trigger a wave of anxiety, as if she were right back in that moment of fear and helplessness.

Nina’s triggers didn’t end there. The smell of alcohol, which had once been a simple reminder of good times spent with friends, now filled her with dread. She found herself avoiding bars altogether and distancing herself from friends who still enjoyed the nightlife. It felt safer to remain at home, cocooned in a world she could control, rather than risk encountering anything or anyone that could remind her of her stalker. The idealized image of happy families she once appreciated now made her feel hollow and isolated, as if those joyful connections were forever out of reach. Every time she saw a family laughing together in a park or on a commercial, a pang of longing would surge through her, amplified by the nagging fear that she might never feel that sense of belonging again.

As Nina sat in her car, parked outside her office, she felt the familiar clench of anxiety grip her throat. It had taken months of turmoil and isolation for her to seek help, to finally confront the shadows that had begun to overshadow her life. She was terrified of being vulnerable, of opening up about her fears and the trauma that had turned her world upside down. Yet, she realized she could no longer bear the weight of this burden alone. While she hoped to reclaim her life and find her way back to the confident, engaging person she used to be, what frightened her most was the possibility that she might never escape the grips of her past.
